problem: Robots in unknown environments must explore, localise and plan at the same time, online. Existing options each fall short. Metric SLAM drifts and has no exploration policy. Frontier exploration is greedy and backtracks a lot. Learned or cross-embodiment navigators (Neural-SLAM, ViKiNG, NoMaD, RECON) need large-scale pre-training or teleoperated pre-mapping of the target environment. Prior Active Inference (AIF) navigators were limited to toy grid worlds or needed pre-training, and each handled only exploration or only goal-reaching.
motivation: Warehouses, homes and outdoor lots often have no prior map and cannot be pre-collected. A single system that needs no pre-training and tolerates drift, perceptual aliasing and sensor failure is therefore valuable. AIF derives both perception (Variational Free Energy minimisation) and action (Expected Free Energy minimisation) from one probabilistic objective. Within that objective, exploration (epistemic value) and goal-seeking (pragmatic value) arise as complementary terms rather than hand-arbitrated modes. The design is also inspired by animal cognitive maps (place-cell vs grid-cell style topological/metric split).
key_idea: Treat navigation as online Bayesian structure learning in a discrete POMDP: a sparse topological graph grows through free-energy model comparison, localisation is variational inference over a factored (topological state, metric position) latent, and actions are chosen by MCTS over Expected Free Energy, so exploration and image-goal reaching come from one objective.
insight: The paper has no component ablations; its evidence is analytical. (1) Separating the discrete state s_t from the metric position p_t lets accumulated displacement disambiguate visually identical places. It also lets the map pre-grow 'predicted' nodes within LiDAR range, which the epistemic term then targets. This gives coverage efficiency comparable to FAEL and far above GBPlanner and Frontiers in large maps (sim large warehouse CE 4.02 vs FAEL 4.65, GBPlanner 1.13, Frontiers 0.60). The gap disappears in small maps (≤80 m²), where LiDAR range already covers most of the area. The same preference for refining nearby predicted nodes causes a coverage plateau around 90%. (2) The drift table shows the belief odometry tracks the sensor odometry (RMSE 1.83 model vs 1.65 sensor), so AIMAPP does not continuously correct drift; it corrects only opportunistically on panorama re-recognition. Its advantage over Frontiers is lower per-metre drift (ATE/m 0.20 vs 0.58), because it backtracks less, plus not depending on a consistent occupancy grid. (3) The goal-reaching path-length ratio (PLR) decomposes multiplicatively: overall 1.260 ≈ plan-vs-A* 1.085 × executed-vs-plan 1.163. Most inefficiency therefore comes from replanning when transitions believed feasible turn out blocked, not from plan quality. The inductive prior H propagates goal utility beyond the MCTS horizon, which yields a forward-sweep-like utility heatmap.
method: Factored generative model: a POMDP with a discrete topological state s_t and a continuous 2D position p_t. It is parameterised by observation likelihood A_o=P(o|s), position likelihood A_p=P(p|s), state transitions B_s and position transitions B_p. Observations are 360° panoramas matched to stored memories with SSIM (65% threshold).

Localisation as VFE minimisation: the posterior over states combines motion prediction and panorama evidence. A Z-score confidence test (threshold 4) decides whether to update A_o (adding extra observations per state, e.g. for lighting changes) or to enter active re-localisation that seeks familiar observations.

Online map expansion by free-energy model comparison: ΔF = F[Â_p] − F[A_p] < 0 adds nodes wherever a predicted position lies outside the influence radius (1 m for envs ≤40 m², else 2 m) of existing nodes. Up to 8 lookahead nodes are hypothesised in LiDAR free directions, and A_o, B_s, B_p are resized.

Transition learning: Dirichlet pseudo-count updates of B_s with situation-dependent rates (forward: experienced ±7, predicted ±5; reverse: ±5 / ±3). Obstacles moved at run time are handled by weakening blocked transitions.

EFE-based planning via MCTS (depth 10, 30 simulations, UCB1 selection) over 13 discrete actions (12 headings + stay). Per-step EFE = info gain on states + info gain on parameters (A_p) + expected collision (binary per-direction LiDAR signal vs preference C_c) + utility on observation, position and state preferences. Policies are selected with softmax(−γG − H).

Inductive prior H: preferences are propagated backwards through B_s^T from goal states, so goals beyond the MCTS horizon still bias action selection. Goal-reaching uses a goal panorama as C_o with pragmatic weight 10.

ROS2 system architecture: the AIF cognitive layer (localisation, mapping, action selection) chooses node goals, while an interchangeable perception front-end and Nav2 motion planner execute and report motion failures. The system runs on a Jetson Orin Nano.

setting.backbone: Discrete-state Active Inference POMDP (topological + metric latent) with MCTS over Expected Free Energy. No neural network; SSIM panorama matching; Nav2 for low-level motion.
setting.training_data: none (no pre-training; model structure and parameters are learned online, self-supervised, from the robot's own sensorimotor experience during each run)
setting.observation: 360° panoramic RGB (stitched from consecutive camera frames in sim; Ricoh Theta X 360° camera on real robot) + 360° 2D LiDAR (range capped at 12 m) + wheel odometry
setting.action_space: 13 discrete actions (12 headings + stay) that move to adjacent topological nodes spaced by an influence radius (1–2 m); executed by the Nav2 motion planner
setting.simulator: Gazebo (ROS2; Amazon warehouse and house worlds, TurtleBot3 Waffle)
setting.privileged: none for exploration. Goal-reaching assumes a known start position (re-localisation bypassed) and a goal image already observed during a prior exploration phase.

numbers_note: No standard embodied-navigation benchmark is used. All environments are custom (Gazebo Amazon warehouse at 3 sizes, a Gazebo house, and three real sites). Split 'test' is a placeholder, since there is no train/val/test split. CE is m²/m and nAUC is a normalised 0-1 value (kept as printed). ExploSR values are printed as fractions (e.g. 0.71) and converted to 0-100; they measure the fraction of attempts needed to get 5 successful exploration trials, not episodic nav success. Coverage curves over distance appear only in figures. The bedroom has no CE table entry. Headline aggregates: '90.3% relative to manual exploration' in sim, and '74% of human-teleoperated performance on average' including real envs. The paper is internally inconsistent on house size (175 m² in main text vs 156 m² in appendix) and real warehouse size (185 vs 186 m²). Human-intervention counts are in an appendix table. Compute: Jetson Orin Nano, 47.5%±16.8% CPU, 36.8%±2.2% RAM, max model 44.9 MB.
results:
Coverage efficiency is comparable to or better than classical exploration planners.
- Sim large warehouse: CE 4.02 (FAEL 4.65, GBPlanner 1.13, Frontiers 0.60).
- Sim house: CE 4.89, above manual (4.02) and GBPlanner/Frontiers (3.70/2.18), close to FAEL (5.23).
- Real warehouse: CE 2.68 vs Frontiers 2.11.
- Averaged over sim envs, AIMAPP reaches 90.3% of manual CE, with a 79% exploration success rate (GBPlanner 87%, Frontiers 52%, FAEL 48%).
- Drift: per-metre drift is about 3× lower than Frontiers (ATE/m 0.20 vs 0.58). AIMAPP keeps running on sandy and carpeted floors where Nav2-based Frontiers fails outright.
- Goal-reaching: median path-length ratio of 1.24 vs A* over 40 runs, and 15/17 real-world goal runs succeed.
limitations: Perception is a proof-of-concept SSIM comparison of panoramas. It is brittle to lighting and scene changes and assumes rough heading consistency. The finite MCTS horizon (only partly offset by the inductive prior) and fixed discretisation (12 headings, fixed influence radius) cause a ~90% coverage plateau and trouble in narrow passages.

There is no continuous drift correction: the belief odometry tracks sensor odometry and corrects only on re-recognition. Severe drift in unexplored areas can corrupt the map, and the kidnapped-robot case with symmetric places is unresolved. Goal-reaching tests assume a known start pose and goals seen during prior exploration.

Evaluation is small-scale (5 runs per env, custom environments, no standard benchmark). Baselines are only non-learning planners, and FAEL/GBPlanner were not run in the real world. There are no ablations of individual EFE terms or model components.
